state.misconception_label: Assumes that an arrow on a number line starts at zero

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: ![Number line with -12 and -7 marked. Starting at -12, follow an arrow pointing to the right labelled +10. Then there is an arrow labelled b pointing to the left, which ends at -7 on the number line.]() What is the value of \( b \) ? I got \( -7 \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you're on a hike and you start at -12 on the number line. You walk 10 steps to the right, then turn around and walk back 5 steps to the left. What position do you end up at? Let's think about how each step affects your final location on the number line.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so if I start at -12 and go right 10 steps, that would be -12 + 10 which is -2, and then if I go left 5 steps from there I'd end up at -7. But wait, is that what the arrow b is showing? I'm confused about whether b is the number of steps I walk or the place I end up at.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think of the arrow labeled b as representing the steps you take, just like on a hike. So if you start at -12 and take 10 steps to the right, you end up at -2. Then, if you turn around and take 5 steps to the left, where would you end up? Let's use our hiking analogy to figure it out.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses a hiking analogy that requires some reasoning, but doesn't directly address the student's core misconception about arrows starting at zero, and by Turn 2 the student shows new confusion about what b represents that isn't resolved by Turn 3's repetition of the same analogy.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses a concrete hiking analogy throughout both turns, grounding the abstract number line operations in the everyday experience of walking forward and backward along a path.
